title: A Healing That Started an Argument
overview: Jesus heals a man on the day of rest, and the dispute that follows leads him to make sweeping claims about his relationship with God.

parts.label: The man at the pool (vv. 1-9a)
parts.note: Bethesda was a large pool by Jerusalem's Sheep Gate, and people believed the first one into the water when it stirred would be healed. Verse 4, which explains that belief, appears only in later copies, and here Jesus skips the pool and heals a man disabled for thirty-eight years with a word.

parts.label: Trouble over a mat (vv. 9b-16)
parts.note: The Sabbath was the weekly day of rest, and carrying a load counted as forbidden work under the rules of the time, so the leaders object. Jesus' later warning to stop sinning does not clearly say the illness was a punishment, and elsewhere in this book he rejects that simple link.

parts.label: My Father is still working (vv. 17-18)
parts.note: Jewish teachers held that God keeps sustaining the world even on the Sabbath, and Jesus says he works the same way. His opponents took this as Jesus putting himself on God's level, and John says it made them want him dead.

parts.label: What the Son is given (vv. 19-30)
parts.note: Jesus says he acts only in step with the Father, yet he has been given God's own powers to give life and to judge. He says that life begins now for those who trust, and he also speaks of a future day when all the dead will rise and face judgment.

parts.label: Witnesses on his side (vv. 31-40)
parts.note: Jewish law required more than one witness, so Jesus names others who back him: John the Baptist, his own miracles, the Father, and the Scriptures his hearers study closely. His complaint is that they search those writings for life but will not come to the one he says they point to.

parts.label: Whose approval matters (vv. 41-47)
parts.note: Jesus says that caring about praise from one another keeps people from seeking God's approval. He claims Moses wrote about him, so Moses, whose law they trust, will be their accuser, because they do not truly believe what Moses wrote.

disagreement: Most Christian traditions read verses 17 to 23 as Jesus sharing God's own nature, while some groups read them as describing a Son uniquely sent and empowered by God but not equal to him.
think: When someone makes big claims about who they are, what kind of evidence would you need before taking them seriously?
